Projects / Lab / OpenFlexure Microscope
N° 28 — Motorised microscopeCERN-OHL-S-2.0
Build it yourself

OpenFlexure Microscope

Open-source design: OpenFlexure (Richard Bowman, Julian Stirling et al.)

An open microscope with three-axis motion. The body with its stage is printed in one piece and the stage moves on flexible plastic hinges (flexures); according to the authors this gives very fine motion over a range of about 10 mm. Each axis is moved by an M3 screw in a brass nut; a 28BYJ-48 stepper motor turns the screw through 2 : 1 gears (there is also a manual version with thumbwheels). A Sangaboard drives the motors, a Raspberry Pi Camera v2 takes the image and a Raspberry Pi 4 sits in a drawer in the stand. The model shows the motorised version with an RMS objective and a tube lens; the lower-cost version uses the Pi camera’s own lens instead of an objective. An LED board lights the sample from above through a diffuser and a condenser. The model is based on the development version v7.0.0-beta5. The microscope is controlled by the authors’ OpenFlexure server software with a web interface, running on the Raspberry Pi.

04 — FAQ
Can I build it with no experience?

Difficulty of this project: Advanced. The project guide takes you through step by step; it is linked under Licence and safety.

Can I buy the kit from you?

No, we sell nothing. You buy the parts directly from suppliers; we compiled the list under What you’ll need from the project’s source files. We may offer a ready-made kit later; if you want to hear about it, leave your email in the form above.

Are you affiliated with the project’s authors?

No. We work from the open documentation of OpenFlexure Microscope (OpenFlexure (Richard Bowman, Julian Stirling et al.), licence CERN-OHL-S-2.0). The authors are not affiliated with us and have not endorsed this page.

What software will I need?

The microscope is controlled by the authors’ OpenFlexure server with a web interface on the Raspberry Pi (GPL-3.0). The software is open source and free; the project guide is linked under Licence and safety.

Is building it suitable for children?

It’s not a toy. The setup contains small parts and electronics; building it is for ages 14 and up, younger children only under adult supervision, for example at school or in a club.

We’re a school or club. What do you offer?

We don’t sell or invoice anything. The lesson with the SO-101 simulation and the worksheet on the For schools page are free; you buy the parts from suppliers following the list we compiled from the project’s source files.
